speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For many of us in the Malay/Muslim community, this conflict is felt especially deeply, because the Palestinian cause is one that holds profound meaning to us.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: But I believe I speak on behalf of all Singaporeans, not just the Malay/Muslims, that we are horrified and saddened by the latest developments in the Middle East.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: What is happening in Gaza is a terrible humanitarian tragedy.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The suffering, forced displacement and loss of innocent civilians we are witnessing is unbearable to many of us, regardless of our ideologies or faiths.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This House first discussed this matter on 6 November 2023, when we strongly condemned the terrorist attacks by Hamas and called for the immediate and unconditional release of all civilian hostages.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It has destroyed Gaza's critical infrastructure, buildings and homes, forcing almost the entire civilian population of Gaza city to flee but with nowhere safe to go.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Then, there is the widespread starvation and deprivation, as the United Nations (UN) has declared, a "man-made famine".

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To compound the tragedy, humanitarian aid has been blocked for months by Israel.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Palestinians, including women and children, have to risk their lives in an active war zone just to get food.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: More than 1,000 have already been killed in violent, chaotic food distributions.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Yet, the Israeli government has chosen to compound this tragedy by moving ahead with settlement projects in the West Bank.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: By any yardstick, the actions by Israel are unjustifiable and may even be a breach of international humanitarian law.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Israel has the right to defend itself, but, as the Prime Minister said back in May, it has now gone too far.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Along with the wider international community, we must express our firm opposition to violations of international law and to unilateral measures that seek to permanently erase the possibility of a two-state solution.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: But for a two-state solution to be viable, Israel must accept a Palestinian state, just as Palestinians must also accept Israel's right to exist.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To this, I would like to offer my assurance that the recognition of a Palestinian State is indeed what Singapore hopes for and something that the Government is working towards.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: That has always been Singapore’s position to ensure enduring peace for the people of Palestine and Israel.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is not a question of if, but when.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We may not recognise Palestine today, but I would like to make clear to Singaporeans that we have not been – and will not be – silent onlookers to the tragedy unfolding in Gaza.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As Minister Vivian mentioned, we will intensify humanitarian assistance to alleviate the suffering of Palestinians.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will also continue to extend practical support to the Palestinian Authority’s capacity-building efforts, in preparation for eventual statehood.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: My thanks also goes to local non-governmental organisations such as Humanity Matters, Rahmatan Lil Alamin Foundation and Mercy Relief.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Together, we are helping to create the conditions for Palestine to recover and eventually meet our criteria for recognition.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I recognise that we feel anguish, dismay and even revulsion and disgust towards Israel’s actions.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, I am heartened that, while we may have different views on what Singapore’s position should be on this matter, we understand that in order to come to a decision as to what is best for Singapore, our foreign policy also has to take into consideration international complexities and our own national interests.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: When I share this in my engagements and dialogues with the community, the majority of them say they understand and many hope to explore other avenues to continue showing support for the Palestinians. : Mr Speaker, I will continue my speech in English.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: But our Malay/Muslim community has shown me that flashes of indignation and outrage can be channelled into compassion and wisdom.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They have galvanised support for humanitarian assistance for the Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Many started nearly two years ago when the conflict first erupted and the community's efforts are still going strong today.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is not an isolated effort, as many Singaporeans from other communities have stepped up too.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, I was glad to see both Muslims and non-Muslims contribute to the Aid for Gaza, organised by the Rahmatan Lil Alamin Foundation (RLAF) in collaboration with the M3@Towns, which has raised more than $2.4 million for Gaza.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since the start of the conflict, RLAF has raised a total of $15 million for Gaza.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Recently, I met the chief executive officer of the Egyptian Red Crescent when RLAF presented a $1 million cheque as part of our donation.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: After all, if we were in their place, we would hope others would extend the same practical and tangible support.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As the Malay saying goes, "Bersatu teguh, bercerai roboh", which loosely means "united we stand, divided we fall".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now have clarifications on the Statements.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Yes, I can see many hands of Members wanting to speak and seek clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have on record about 16 Members who have filed Parliamentary Questions (PQs) on this subject.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will give priority to these 16 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But first, I would like to take this opportunity to remind Members that pursuant to Standing Order 23, Members may seek clarification on the Ministerial Statements, but no debate should be allowed thereon.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And Members can seek clarifications by way of asking questions, so I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise, and likewise, I ask the Ministers to also keep your answers clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think that one of the reasons the other countries have changed their position is they believe some of the actions that Israel will be taking now will make it much more difficult to have a two-state solution, including the current Israeli government's statement that it will not recognise a state of Palestine, as well as expanding settlements in the West Bank.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What these other governments believe is recognising a state of Palestine now will help to preserve the hope of a two-state solution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is this something that Singapore would consider as well, if it feels the actions of the Israeli government may be undermining the two-state solution?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Actually, all of us are on the same side.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: When I say "all of us", I also include the other countries who have shifted their position.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We all want an immediate release of all the hostages.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We all believe that a two-state solution, as difficult and remote as it is, is the only viable way out of this quagmire.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Where we differ is that every country has its own national circumstances, its own domestic constituencies, its own outlook on its leverage or lack thereof, on the key players in the Middle East.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In the case of Singapore, as I said just now, we pursue foreign policy in a realist mode and we do pay attention to objective reality.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And the first problem which I tried to outline just now is, who is in charge in Palestine?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Are you dealing with Hamas, dealing with the Palestinian Authority or something in Kuwait that has yet to emerge?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, that is the first point, objective reality.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But having said that, the Member also raised the point, and many others have as well, that the current Israeli government is actually making things worse.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The settlement expansion, even their explicit remarks, so both in terms of what they say and what they do, that it is clear that the extremist elements within the Israeli body politic are trying to extinguish prospects for a two-state solution.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, the point is to focus on the similarities that we are all on the same side, but each country will have a different trigger, different threshold and a different appreciation of the situation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party's position on the formal recognition of the state of Palestine is clear in our manifesto, the same manifesto we took to voters before the elections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the earlier remarks by the Minister, going through what had happened in the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With that as a preamble, does the Minister not agree that the prospects of having an effective Palestinian government in place, which is a precondition to Singapore recognising the state of Palestine is not a realistic precondition anymore, given the statement of the Israeli Prime Minister that there will not be a Palestinian state, and one can assume that he will work overtime to make sure that does not happen, and that is separate to the signing of an expanded settlement agreement that would bisect the occupied West Bank.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And in this regard, what specific principles are we upholding by not recognising the state of Palestine forthwith?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should recognising the state of Palestine not be in our national interest and more weight placed instead on Israel's flagrant violations of international law and commitment to continue doing the same?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would not doing so send a clear message that as a matter of clear principle, Singapore's foreign policy stands for the foundational role of the UN in maintaining peace and security, and does not stand for breaches of international law, particularly in view of the Government's public comments on UNSC Resolution 242, and separately, UNSC Resolution 2334?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government, and this was a part of my PQ, reviewed whether close ties with Israel, particularly in the military domain going forward, continue to be in our national interest?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And has the Government assessed whether Singapore is relatively over-invested in the Israel-Singapore relationship, and is it not time to diversify in our national interest?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister spoke of sanctions and announced that more details would be announced later.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Do the sanctions that the Minister is foreseeing have any impact on current military-to-military relationship with Israel?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My last question is to the Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Government see a direct link to threats to Singapore, given close Singapore-Israel ties in the immediate to medium term?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: First question: is our requirement that there be an effective political entity or government on the other side a realistic one?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Leader of the Opposition adds on to say, well, Israel will do its best to make sure that there is no realistic government.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Therefore, by insisting on having an effective government, as an objective reality, are we setting the bar too high?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I reminded you the two-state solution did not begin yesterday.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, it goes back to the UN in 1947.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Israel took what was on offer, ran and declared independence.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The entire constellation of Arab countries said no.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It was only in 1988 that the Palestinian Liberation Organization, in its proclamation of a Palestinian state, even then, only implicitly recognised Israel's right to exist and renounced terrorism.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We welcomed the proclamation because these two elements, recognising the other exists and renouncing terrorism, are important for our national interest.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I also then went on to describe the events – Oslo, the elections in Gaza, the two decades without election, the violence between Hamas and Fatah – again, to point out the lack of an objective reality is not all on and due to one other party.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They have got to get their own house in order.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Will we allow, however, Israel, therefore, to have a veto?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The answer is we cannot allow them to have a veto because our consistent long-held belief is a two-state solution.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If either one or both says no, we cannot go along with them on that ride.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Member asked whether we are being anachronistic because several, basically, European powers in the last few days have changed their position.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In my answer to Mr Vikram Nair, I tried to remind everyone that in the big picture, we all want the same thing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But different countries will have different thresholds, different triggers to decide when they take certain diplomatic moves.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We, for now, have shifted since May last year.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We said we are prepared, in principle, to recognise the Palestinian state.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is a shift, but it is also a shift, which I want to emphasise, recognises that you have to clear a certain bar – that amongst the Palestinians themselves, they have sorted out themselves politically to be an effective, unified voice that can conduct foreign policy, that can enter into agreements and make agreements stick – and also because of our complete aversion to terrorism.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is why we have taken the current position.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not think we are being anachronistic.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think we are being realistic, given the circumstances in which Singapore has to operate in our part of the world.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: On defence, I have already said that yes, it is not a secret that they played a role in our early years, for which we are grateful, and they continue to have an invaluable role.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But again, that does not mean that we are locked into giving them a free pass.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: When you have an equal and mutually respectful partnership, when you differ, you must be prepared to say so, to say so openly, candidly and constructively.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I will not get into operational details of defence.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You know that it is the Government's established long-standing policy not to publicly diverse divulge details on defence cooperation for national security reasons.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Singapore will not allow itself to be held hostage.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Beyond that, I am not going to get into operational details.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: As a National Serviceman yourself, I am sure you understand that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If you look at the issue of radicalisation, there are many factors that account for it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There are also many incidents around the world that are happening – not only the incidents, but also what our young people and Singaporeans come across on social media and what they read.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I can say that we are very fortunate to have not only enforcement agencies that really look at how we can minimise or eradicate, if possible, the issue of radicalisation, but we have community partners that work together with us to go upstream and look at how we can manage this and help our people in promoting a harmonious and peaceful living here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, I tried to think what the Leader of the Opposition is suggesting when he asked that question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Is he suggesting that our policy stance has resulted in radicalisation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I just want to get his answer to that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My query to the Senior Minister of State pertains to the threat landscape and the environment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In 2013, I shared with this House that there is a concern if Singapore's position may have an impact on the way people think about this particular issue, if we are seen as too close to the Israeli position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because we have had episodes in the past, and the MHA had announced it, where certain individuals are held under the Internal Security Act and they cite this issue as one reason for their thoughts and actions insofar as planning violence in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: What is key is that the security agencies will look at all the different areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Certain things may have an effect or perceived effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nevertheless, in Singapore, I am sure you are familiar about how we build our nation and what we do, we understand there are various things that affect how a person thinks; how that will evoke emotion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: What we do is we work with community partners and agencies, and if you read what the religious rehabilitation groups are doing, they not only look at the Malay/Muslim issues, but they look at how they can play a part in building a peaceful, harmonious and progressive Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, at the end of the day, looking at Singapore's interests, linking back to what Minister Vivian has said earlier, I want to reiterate that the issue of radicalisation comes from various factors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Also, if you look at the profile of the different individuals who have been so called radicalised and are at the early stage or even at the advance stage of radicalisation, there are various factors that account for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To pin down to just our policy stance will not be accurate.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: How can the Government better communicate the Government's approach and that this approach is the best one for Singapore?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I would ask for time to let us sort out the details of the announcements.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The larger point behind that, is that, this is an expression of disapproval.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: On international law, I think that is very clear.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Because of our own circumstances, we do have to abide by and we do need to comply with international law.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But it is also equally important for us all to understand the difference between international law and domestic law is that you can have a court, in this case, the International Court of Justice; in our case, we have our own domestic courts.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Internationally, enforcement actually depends on consent from all the states involved.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I say this so that, first, we get a realistic appreciation of the limits of international law, but we also understand why, as a small nation, we cannot operate on the basis of "might is right" and give in to that every time someone invokes that, because that is inimical to our own interest.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But let me just bring the deliberations today back and also partially refer to what the Leader of the Opposition was asking my colleague.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Singapore has to start with a realistic appreciation of who we are, which means, in particular, multiracial, multi-religious, in Southeast Asia, in a part of the world which used to be tumultuous and could be if things unravel further.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And who we are also means we are exposed to external events and external influence, and that is a reality.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, we start with a realistic appreciation of our circumstances.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is easy to state that, but on every issue, we have to triangulate between these three poles – what is in our national interest for security, what is in our national interest for unity and what is in our national interest to maintain international law.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And sometimes, there is tension between these three poles and the way we have to address it and the way the PAP government has addressed it, is that when these tensions are evident, we talk about it constructively, openly, delicately.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We do not use it to score domestic political points or to split our society in order to get short-term political points.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, the larger point I am trying to tell all of us is that the world is messy and the world has become far, far more dangerous and it will be increasingly more and more difficult for Singapore to just jealously guard its national interests while keeping everybody together.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And we make our decisions in our own national interest; it means we will not always follow the crowd.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Many times, we will be in a minority and we will not be afraid to be in a minority, so long as we understand that we are taking a stand based on principle, we are taking a stand to defend our own people's welfare and security, and that when we deal with thorny issues, we will discuss it openly, respectfully and constructively.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Member's question, is there a risk that all these events outside Singapore can radicalise our own people?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Is this the only source of division, radicalisation and extremism in the world?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There are other parts of the world which can also sow division, discord and extremism in the world.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Is this something which we can resolve once and for all with a discussion, a Ministerial Statement or a debate in Parliament?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This is always going to be a work-in-progress.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And on that note, I just want to make this appeal, also to the Leader of the Opposition – this is one of those times we need to make common cause.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Member and I may differ on the timing of recognition but in the same way, as I describe our position vis-a-vis the other countries, I think we all ultimately want the same thing: we want peace.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We want mutual respect between people with complicated histories and identity.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And we want to be able to do good where we can, by working with as many parties, as many entities as possible.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, this should be an occasion for unity amidst the difficulty and we should be very mindful in our conversations, not just in this House, but outside this House, that we secure unity, security and peace under international law.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is possible and I still want to hold on to that prospect.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: When we go to the Middle East, and Members, Mr Gerald Giam was with me, I could tell the Israelis and even the Arabs, "if you want a one-state solution, your delegation, your government must look like mine." Everyone nods and yet, also in their heart of hearts, they know, it is not possible.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Well, if it is not possible, that is why you need a two-state solution.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But on the other hand, we should also be grateful for what we have in Singapore, but also understand it is always at risk, always fragile and we need to jealously protect it and guard it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's aid to Gaza demonstrates our compassion for Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also signals our values as a principle of small states.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How effective has Singapore's humanitarian assistance been in meeting the needs of Gaza?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My second clarification is this: the International Association of Genocide Scholars has declared that Israel's actions in Gaza are consistent with the legal definition of genocide.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I cannot attest to what happens once it gets into Gaza, but I take the following attitude.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: One, gratitude to Singaporeans for generosity, for expressing compassion in a very real way and the fact that the funds raised were raised in a multi-religious, multiracial effort.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is a very Singaporean expression of compassion, that is first.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Two, I am grateful it was the SAF that played a major role in the delivery, and I thank the SAF men and women.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Three, I am grateful that over the six decades, we have built close, respectful and constructive ties across all the countries in the Middle East, so we can base our air force in Jordan, we can overfly Israel, we can airdrop in Palestine, we can work with our Egyptian partners, whether to hand over money or humanitarian assistance and, right now, as I outlined just now, work with Egyptian hospitals to look after people who need medical care and I mentioned even community policing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Well, this sort of project, which we are doing together with Japan to train police officers working under the Palestinian Authority to prepare for future statehood.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, there is a lot to be grateful for and to also reflect on the blessings that we have in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is a very Singaporean expression of compassion in action.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not think they have fully heard the arguments on merit and they certainly have not arrived at the verdict, but we will have to wait for that and to act accordingly.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I can share with the Member what I told the Israeli President – and the delegation Members who were with me can attest to that – because we are friends, we also have a duty to be candid.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And as I told him, "It is true that the world has double standards and the world expects more of Israel, because Israel was born from the ashes of the Holocaust.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And if Israel loses its international moral standing authority, that does untold strategic damage to your long-term prospects." They did not push back on that point because they know it is a sincerely held view from someone who hopes for peace for them and their neighbouring people who, even in the darkest of times, have to hope.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They need hope that there is a better way.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But again, be grateful for what we have in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I have one clarification to the Minister for Foreign Affairs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister shared that shift in position on the targeted sanctions on the settler groups and individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, I am thankful to the Minister for sharing that slight change, because if you look at the European Union (EU), the US, Canada, Australia, Japan and the United Kingdom (UK), they also did similar targeted sanctions back in 2024.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, Singapore shifting in 2025 is, in some ways, not taken very lightly and probably a very principled move, especially when Singapore is a financial hub and seen as a financial centre.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But my clarification is, Minister, in a broader perspective, the threshold of taking broader sanctions on Israel, the entity or the country itself, can the Minister share how Singapore would assess the actions of other countries, going forward, that have imposed financial or economic sanctions on Israel and whether there is scope for us to consider similar enhancement measures in a calibrated way?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Only in a situation where the Gaza situation does not abate, how would we take that into consideration and how would be our principled assessment be?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my question is, in fact, about the thresholds: what would be our principled guidelines to shift to a different threshold on broader sanctions?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But let us also not assume or presume that sanctions will make a major difference to facts on the ground.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I say this not just with respect to what we are proposing for the settler groups, but again, the world's history on sanctions and their effectivity, I would say, it is often more a statement of principle and expression of disapproval.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I would not bank that, historically, any set of sanctions have been decisive in its own way.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, like many things in foreign policy, it is a multivariate equation and, sometimes, you need all the different pieces, the configuration, to come together in time and space for there to be a step change.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My clarification is borne out of my understanding of the three Ministerial Statements that, in fact, we do have two levels of agency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is diplomacy and accessibility that our MFA has in the region.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I feel humbly proud, if that is the correct word to use, that we have two excellent institutions with major agency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we use the agencies of diplomacy, in the form of MFA and humanitarian assistance in the form of SAF, to bring about one step closer to peace in the region?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am always pleasantly surprised or gratified by the access that we have.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: My conclusion, after years in this is, people give us access because, one, they have heard of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They have heard of Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They hear our Prime Ministers, both what they say domestically and internationally, it travels; and it is credible.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They know we are a united country and united across race, language and religion.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They now, as Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim said just now, when we say something, we actually take it seriously, we commit to it and we deliver.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They do not expect us to completely echo their positions.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, they know that we are serious-minded, we are careful, we are deliberate and we do not just follow the crowd.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And that is precisely why I think we get access and why we get at least applied hearing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And where we can make common calls and where we can sign agreements and do things together, we do.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And Singapore and Singaporeans are welcome throughout, even troubled spots, because of this reputation.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But at the same time, we also should retain a sense of realism and humility.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We cannot solve very difficult, thorny issues all over the world, to the extent that we can extend our friendship, our support, our humanitarian assistance, if they want to use us sometimes officially or unofficially, as a venue, we are happy to pour tea.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But we should never, never overestimate our abilities to deal with very difficult issues globally.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, I am quite content to play a constructive and useful role, but not to be made use of.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: At the same time, bearing in mind that the moment Singapore fails or is disunited, or that the leaders of Singapore no longer credible, it is game over.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In other words, it is not so much exactly the details of your decision but the basis by which we organise ourselves, arrive at decisions, make commitments, stick to commitments, deliver the goods and behave in a consistent, constructive law-abiding way.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not want to use the word "moral" where states are concerned, but Members know what I mean.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There is a certain code by which people know Singapore will always behave.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And for that, they will accept that we will be different from time to time.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But it is respect and we can do some good and that is the way I conduct our relations with other countries.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On that note, I know that many people disagree with Israel's actions in Gaza and the West Bank.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not just a matter of national security, but also a matter of national conscience. : In terms of our interests, Sir, it is not just a matter of national security for us in Singapore but arguably also a question of national conscience as many have expressed very strong views.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Minister has, in his answer to the hon Member Mr Saktiandi Supaat earlier mentioned that sanctions have not always proven to be effective.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I seek the Minister's views and how we can re-envision these sanctions could impact Israel, Palestine as well as other actors, for example, the US.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am grateful for the Member's questions and I appreciate where she is coming from.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But again, I want to urge a sense of realism.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Will sanctions from a small city-state, like Singapore, move the needle on its own?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But is it an expression of our views?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Oh, I am sure they will notice it, precisely because they know that we are careful, deliberative, constructive partners who want the best for their long-term survival and for their neighbours, the Palestinians.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, we should be realistic about what we say and do and the effect of what we say and do.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: On open lines of communication, on ceasefire negotiations, I want to give full credit to our friends in Qatar and Egypt.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And in the case of Qatar, even facing danger for being a venue for such negotiations and we should give them our fullest support, appreciation and respect for doing that.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not see that in the imminent future.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Again, we need to understand the nature of conflicts in diplomacy, that the most effective peacemakers have to be both trusted by both sides and have leverage because the world is not short of conference venues where people can meet and have a nice cup of tea.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But it needs to be a place where both sides feel that they are safe and that you are not playing games.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But very often, to force two sides which are very far away, apart from each other and sometimes, to be honest, even having sub-segments of the two sides who are working across purposes, we need leverage.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, again my plea is, be realistic about what we can do, what we should do.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I accept the Member's point that our words and our actions should reflect what we stand for and we cannot close our eyes and close our ears and keep silent when things are clearly wrong and unconscionable.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I hope I have made the point that we have not been such a party.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We are all weather friends, but we are also friends who tell you hard truth.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: To the extent that we can help, we will help, but we will not push and overstay our welcome or overestimate our ability to solve problems which have defied solutions for decades, centuries or, sometimes, millennia.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan, you also had a PQ on this for tomorrow's Sitting.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Speaker, I have a clarification for the Minister, similar to hon colleagues Mr Saktiandi and Ms Nadia.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It is a question about sanctions, but I would like to go specifically to the context, also of the question I have filed, which is regarding Israel's attack in Qatar.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: How does Singapore's response in this instance to Israel's attack in Qatar compute, vis-a-vis our responses to past instances of violation of sovereignty?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Can we not consider imposing sanctions, as an expression of our disapproval, to a violation of this very core principle of international law?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And we stand on that again, because again, the same question went through my mind, what if it happened here, what would we do and what would we say?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Again, for Qatar, the US' largest airbase in the Middle East is in Qatar.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The real player who could and should have ensured security – I do not want to cause more problems, but we can think about that.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Again, my larger point I am making to all of us, please have a realistic view of what Singapore can and cannot do.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: My own view is with the Qataris, we were in contact immediately.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They know where we stand, they appreciated our stand.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But there are some much bigger players who need to resolve the very awkward set of questions that the attack posed.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But also, let us bear in mind that this is a dangerous and unpredictable world.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Again, at some risk, I will also tell you that there are offices of terrorist organisations in our region.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is an objective reality and we need to be mindful and we need to be careful.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We do not want to say too much, but there are some things which we need to be aware of and we need to take appropriate precautions from.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Maybe you should ask Minister Shanmugam about that.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister stated that Singapore will reconsider its position on recognising the Palestinian state if the situation continues to deteriorate or if Israel takes any further steps to extinguish the two-state solution.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the continued expansion of Israeli settlements, the Israeli government's stated policy that "there will be no Palestinian state" and even their alleged targeting of peace negotiators in Qatar, does the Minister not consider these to be severe enough to trigger a re-evaluation of Singapore's position now?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, the Minister said that Singapore will recognise Palestine when it has an effective government that accepts Israel's right to exist and categorically renounces terrorism.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But the Palestinian Authority has already made a commitment to renounce terrorism and carry out reforms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What additional steps does the Palestinian Authority need to take in order for Singapore to recognise the state of Palestine?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I have set out for all of us our principal considerations and the variables which we are watching.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not want to jump the gun and enter into excessively hypothetical discussions.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The second question was what else is necessary for the Palestinian Authority.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I wish they were in charge in Gaza, but you and I know they are not, or certainly not yet.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But we continue to work with them, we continue to build up their capacity, we continue to prepare them for eventual statehood and for the time when they can be in charge.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I should also add, if you read carefully all the statements of those who have apparently changed position in the last few days, I very seriously doubt any of them can actually begin the actual process or normalisation as long as hostages are still held in the tunnels of Gaza.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think the best way to understand this is everyone wants the same endpoint, but there can be arguments about when and how the route you take to reach the ultimate destination.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have had almost an hour of clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have called on every Member who had filed questions on this except for two – Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And now, I will call on Mr Sharael Taha.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I appreciate the position has evolved, given the deteriorating circumstances.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, many may find it hard to understand the preconditions and could approach it from a very binary stand – either we support or we do not support – which can lead to a lot of misunderstanding, especially when other countries have had their individual separate reasons for doing so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My question to the Minister is, how can we better communicate this position of ours so that there is no misunderstanding within the country and with other countries?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My second supplementary question is to the Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and I will ask the supplementary question in Malay. :   It is extremely difficult and heartbreaking to witness the suffering and loss of innocent lives in Gaza and we have provided substantial assistance to them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How can Singapore and Singaporeans continue to help those in Palestine?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And how can we also put an end to this suffering, call for a ceasefire, provide immediate humanitarian aid to victims in Gaza and work with other countries to find a lasting and peaceful solution for the Palestinian people?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This has been longer than my Committee of Supply and the question is how to communicate better.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is why we have always supported the Palestinians' right to self-determination and their own homeland.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is why "from the river to the sea" is not possible for either party.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They have to find the wisdom and the leadership to create a two-state solution where they can live in peace and security.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Number three, whilst we recognise Israel's right to exist and we recognise Israel's need to be strong, there is also wisdom in knowing how to use your strengths.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You can win a tactical victory and lose the strategic war.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: What it is worth, this is what we are telling the Israelis and have been doing so for some time.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Next point, we know that anything Singapore says or does is not going to resolve the situation on the ground in the Middle East.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But for what it is worth, we will express a stand which is consistent with our own identity and values as a multiracial, multi-religious state.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We hope and wait and will support and take efforts to hopefully make that an objective reality.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In the meantime, we have targeted sanctions to express our disapproval for further moves to make a two-state solution impossible.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is my "too long, did not read" (TLDR) summary of the last two hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: (In Malay):   I thank Mr Sharael for the question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If we look back to the moment when this situation unfolded, we can see that the Malay/Muslim community wanted to contribute to efforts to ease the suffering that was taking place over there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We started with our members and organisations who stepped forward to contribute donations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We also held special prayers, as you may recall, and even now, whenever we perform the prayers, we include the Qunut Nazilah, or Supplication During Calamity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This demonstrates the enduring resilience that I observe in our Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We also joined other communities to take action in providing support, humanitarian aid, as well as establishing solid and safe platforms that provided a space for our needs during these difficult times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Minister Vivian has also shared, or briefly outlined, what we have done and will continue to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will also provide support to hospitals, and medical supplies, as well as enhance their capabilities over there, not only for the Palestinian Authority, but also for those who wish to study through scholarships for new students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: All of this is provided by the Government as well as Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We also understand that the situation there remains volatile, so we will continue to monitor it and if there are opportunities, we will increase and multiply our efforts and further enhance assistance to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is the commitment that Minister Vivian and the Singapore Government have made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I hope that together we can seize this opportunity to build our united nation and while we may be affected by incidents abroad, we must prioritise our nation's interests across all aspects of policy and our collective lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I am heartened when I observed, through my involvement in community work and serving in several ministries, how the Government balances Singapore's interests while prioritising the needs of our multi-racial society, including the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: What I witness is truly remarkable, as I have not seen other governments having similar principles and policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I hope that together we can build Singapore, not just as a multi-racial society, but as an extraordinary and unique country that can achieve not only our national goals, but provide opportunities for all races, religions and every individual so they can progress and become the best version of themselves.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We voted for it because we look at it in totality.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This is something which we support, or which we want to happen, which we hope will happen, even if, as I said, the objective reality has not yet occurred.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Hostages are still being held in tunnels, Hamas is still in power in Gaza.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Nevertheless, we voted in favour of it because we think this solution encapsulates the full width of measures needed in the long run for hopefully peace to come to this region, so hence our vote.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I can assure you our votes in the UN are never performative or cynical.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We do so on the basis of principle and of a careful assessment of our national interest.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Order of the Day.
